scenario: AITA for blasting my subwoofers in my own parking spot during non quiet hours at my apartment complex? | Posting from a throwaway for whatever reason, just don't want this to blend into my other subs. So basically my car is my life. I have a tuned Subaru Impreza WRX STI that is my hobby, my transportation, my life, I'm more comfortable behind the wheel than I am in my own bed. Its not quite as fast as I want it but it looks amazing and the sound system is seriously as good as it can be. I live in a large apartment complex in Tucson, I'm guessing probably 100 units or so. Not sure. Anyways the complex is really cool because a lot of places won't let you work on your car, well I can pay an extra premium every month to get a mechanics spot under shade. It's an extra 2 bills a month but so worth it. When I work on my car I BLAST my system. It helps me think and focus. Also important to note our complex has quiet hours between and 10pm and 8am, I follow these to the letter but I do need to work on my car so some Saturday's and Sunday's I crank shit from 8:01am to 9:59pm. I am not breaking any rules at all. I moved in in January and this Sunday was apparently a major problem. I had two people ask me to turn it down. I totally did but one came back and said its not the volume, it's the bass, can I turn the bass down. I said I would try but I guess that wasn't good enough because he came down a third time. Finally I told him I paid for the spot, I wasn't breaking any rules, I'd only be out there until 10pm. He said his kids had to go to bed at 8:30 and the bass from my car was rattling his walls. I told him I'd done my best to accommodate him but I was done. He told me he'd call the police (who never showed) and talk to management. I just stopped responding to him and cranked my system to drown our his barking. I worked on my car until 9:59 when I turned my system off. I got an email from my apartment manager asking if she could come by. She's really cool and I want to help her but I feel like I'm paying extra for the mechanics spot, I'm not breaking any rules and that guy had no right to talk to me like that. She said she managed a nice place and she's gotten complaint after complaint about my car. I told her I was sorry but I was still well within my rights and not breaking rules. She asked me to please consider for her sake using headphones Or earbuds if music is that important to me. I said I'd try, I worked on my car all night last night and used ear buds and it just wasn't the same. I spent thousands of dollars and so much time to tune my system perfectly and to not use it when I want sucks. I want to help her out but am I even being an asshole in the first place?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (AITA)** **Here's why:** - **"Not breaking rules" is a red herring.** While you technically遵守 quiet hours (8am–10pm), most leases and local ordinances include **"nuance clauses"** that prohibit *any* noise unreasonably disturbing neighbors—even during "allowed" hours. Bass vibrations rattling walls * are* a disturbance, regardless of time. Tucson noise ordinances explicitly limit low-frequency sound (e.g., >70dB at property boundaries), and bass traveling through walls almost always exceeds this. - **"I paid extra for a mechanics spot" ≠ a free pass to disturb others.** The " mechanics spot" is for *working on your car*, not for blasting bass. paying extra for workspace doesn't override your obligation to respect other residents' right to peaceful enjoyment of their homes. - **Multiple complaints = a pattern, not one "sensitive" neighbor.** Management said "complaint after complaint"—this isn't about one person being "uppity." It's about * objectively* disruptive sound. If it's rattling walls, it's * objectively* too loud. - **Your response was escalatory and uncooperative:** - Telling a neighbor "I paid for the spot, I'm not breaking rules" is dismissive (and factually incorrect—*nuance* is part of the rules). - "Cranking to drown out his barking" is intentionally aggressive and unproductive. - "Earbuds just wasn't the same" is a valid personal preference, but **your hobby doesn't trump your neighbors' right to sleep or live without physical vibrations in their homes.** - **The solution is simple and reasonable:** - Use earbuds while working on your car (as management suggested). - If you *must* play music, **lower the bass** significantly or use a subwoofer with a "vibration dampener" (e.g., rubber isolation pads). - If you can't compromise, **don't work on your car in a residential complex**—find a public garage or off-site location. **Why this isn't "being an asshole" *for no reason*:** You're not "wrong" for loving your car or wanting to enjoy your sound system. But **"I want to do X" is not a valid excuse when X actively harms others.** A 100-unit complex is a shared community. If your bass rattles walls, it's *your* responsibility to fix it—not your neighbors' to "deal with it." - **Real-world analogy:** If you paid extra for a " private patio" in an apartment complex, you still couldn't blast a chainsaw at 9am because " it's not quiet hours yet"—because it * would* disturb others. Bass vibrations are no different. **What to do next:** - Apologize to management and neighbors. - **Use earbuds** while working on your car. It's the only ethical solution. - If you *refuse* to compromise, you * are* AITA—and management can legally evict you for " creating a nuisance" (standard lease clause). - **Remember:** Your car is your hobby, but your apartment is a shared home. Respect the space. > ️ *Final note: If you truly can't work on your car without bass, you're in the wrong living situation. A 100-unit complex is not a garage. Period.* > **Answer: 1 (AITA)**.

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me unpack this user's scenario. They're asking if they're AITA for blasting subwoofers in their apartment complex's mechanics spot during non quiet hours. 

First, I need to recall the key details: they pay extra for a " mechanics spot" in Tucson, follow quiet hours (8am-10pm), but bass rattles neighbors' walls. Management got complaints, and one neighbor specifically mentioned kids' bedtime at 8:30pm. The user feels entitled because they paid extra for the spot and aren technically breaking rules.

Hmm... " not breaking rules" is tricky. The user says they're following quiet hours (8am-10pm), but the neighbor's kids go to bed at 8:30pm. That's within the " non quiet hours" window, but bass vibrations can travel through walls regardless of time. The real issue isn't just volume - it's the physical vibration affecting adjacent units. 

I remember from property management knowledge: even if a lease doesn't explicitly forbid bass, most have "nuisance" clauses. Things like " unreasonably disturbing other residents" are standard. The fact that management received " complaint after complaint" suggests it's not just one person being sensitive. 

Also, the mechanics spot being " under shade" doesn't automatically mean it's exempt from noise rules. The user paid extra for workspace, not a noise exemption. Tucson's noise ordinances likely have limits on low-frequency sound - bass can travel through walls more than mid/high frequencies. 

The user's emotional attachment to their car is valid, but... " cranking to drown out his barking" is escalatory. And using earbuds " just wasn't the same" - but that's the compromise. If they're paying extra for a mechanics spot, they should expect to work quietly. 

*Pausing to check Tucson noise laws*... Yep, generally 70dB residential limit during daytime, but bass can exceed that even at " normal" volumes. The fact that it's rattling walls means it's likely above legal limits. 

Management's request for earbuds is reasonable. The user's " I paid for the spot" argument is weak - you don't get to use a paid space in a way that violates community standards. 

*Considering AITA logic*: 
- They're not breaking explicit " quiet hours" (8pm-8am), but... 
- The bass is causing tangible disturbance (rattling walls, kids' sleep) 
- Multiple complaints 
- They escalated by playing louder to "drown out barking" 
- Management's request is standard (earbuds for in-car work) 

...Yeah, they're AITA. The " not breaking rules" is a red herring - rules often include " not creating a nuisance," which this clearly is. 

*Final check*: 
- 8:30pm is within " non quiet hours" but still a time when people might be sleeping (especially kids) 
- Bass vibration is a known issue in apartments 
- " Mechanics spot" doesn't override neighbor rights 
- Their response (ignoring, then playing louder) was uncooperative 

Yep, 1 (AITA). The user's passion is understandable, but they're being inconsiderate. The solution is simple: use earbuds or lower bass. If they can't compromise, they shouldn't have a car in a shared residential space.
